name: Crowd-Aware Evacuation Planner
pitch: Plans building evacuations that account for crowds, fire and smoke, tested on simulation.
description: A capstone research project (Team 212) that decides which exit each person should use in a fire. It books capacity on corridors, doors and stairs ahead of time, uses a hybrid ML model for crossing times, and is tested on a seeded simulator calibrated on real crowd data, with a campus and a hospital building.
hardestProblem: TODO: confirm. Best-documented candidate: making the ML delay model trustworthy on real people. Pure ML scored 7.16 s error on real crowd data; calibrating the simulator and learning only a correction to a physics formula brought it to 2.12 s.
results: Look-ahead planning beat shortest-safe-path significantly in 8 of 10 campus scenarios; up to about 36% faster last-out (200 people on floor 3: 367 s to 234 s).
ML crossing-time error 4.76 s to 2.41 s on 784,014 held-out simulated crossings; 2.12 s on 1,813 real crossings (hybrid model).
Transferred to a 124-node hospital building: faster walking-crowd exit in 6 of 6 scenarios.
Gain came from coordination, not prediction accuracy.
highlights: Built a seeded evacuation simulator and five routing methods in Python (NetworkX, NumPy); a look-ahead capacity-booking planner cut last-out time up to 36% vs shortest-safe-path, significant in 8 of 10 campus scenarios over 2,766 runs.

Trained a hybrid LightGBM model (physics formula x learned correction) on 784,014 simulated crossings; halved held-out error (4.76 s to 2.41 s) and reached 2.12 s error on real crowd data where pure ML scored 7.16 s.
Calibrated the simulator on real Juelich crowd measurements, raising door flow from 32%-38% to 98%-122% of lab values, and checked stair speed against NIST drill data.

Showed the method transfers to a second building (100-bed hospital graph, 124 nodes): faster walking-crowd evacuation in 6 of 6 scenarios; identified the ramp as the single point of failure (42 people stranded if blocked in a fire).
Optimised the planner with A* and cached edge costs (median 5.3x faster); it re-plans 2,000 people on a 452-node campus in 1.06 s.

name: Ride Sharing DBMS
pitch: A college ride-sharing system where the rules live in the database: stored procedures, triggers and transaction-safe booking.
description: A DBMS course mini-project: passengers and drivers from different colleges create rides, book seats, pay, rate each other and see their ride history. The interesting part is the MySQL layer. Booking, payment, completion and cancellation are stored procedures, fares and seat checks are functions, triggers keep the ride history audited, and views give driver, passenger and payment summaries. A small Node.js and Express API and a plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript front end sit on top.
hardestProblem: Stopping two people booking the last seat at the same time. Booking runs inside a transaction that locks the ride's row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), checks the seats left, and only then writes the booking, so a ride can't be overbooked.
highlights: 8 tables (college, passenger, vehicle, driver, ride, payment, rating, ride history), 8 stored procedures, 5 functions, 5 triggers and 4 views
Row locking and COMMIT/ROLLBACK for safe seat booking
Triggers write a ride-history audit trail when a ride is created or its status changes
REST API with 9 endpoints for rides, booking, completion, ratings, passengers and drivers

name: Political Bias Detection
pitch: Reads a news headline, says whether it leans left, right or centre, and shows the words that drove the call.
description: A Social Computing course mini-project, done in a team of two. Headlines are turned into sentence embeddings, a classifier learns Left, Center and Right from labelled Kaggle datasets, and SHAP shows which words pushed a prediction. A Gradio app lets you upload training CSVs, train, type a headline and see the prediction, its confidence, a word-importance plot and the most similar headlines it was trained on. The proposal and literature survey are written up in the course slides; the notebook is the working prototype.
hardestProblem: Making the answer explainable instead of a bare label. The proposal argued that most bias detectors are black boxes and learn a publisher's style rather than real bias, so the prototype pairs every prediction with a SHAP word-importance plot and nearest training examples.
highlights: Literature survey of eight papers on political-bias detection, with gaps identified in each
Prototype: MiniLM embeddings with logistic regression (class-balanced) and a nearest-neighbour lookup for similar headlines
SHAP word-level explanations and a Gradio interface for training and testing
Original plan was to fine-tune BERT and predict framing, sensationalism and loaded language; the notebook is the simpler first version
